newsitem.title: USA: November U.S. CPI confirms inflation still tame.
newsitem.headline: November U.S. CPI confirms inflation still tame.

text.p: U.S. retail inflation remains low, resisting upward pressure from wages and energy prices, according to the November consumer price index (CPI) report.

With the economy widely expected to decelerate in coming months, inflation should remain a comforting indicator for consumers and policymakers, even as analysts complain of boredom over stubbornly stable prices.
"The inflation reports are getting to be a bit of a bore, but that's good news, because it suggests inflation is well in check," said Robert Dederick of Northern Trust.

The Labor Department reported CPI rose 0.3 percent in November and 0.2 percent on the core rate, excluding volatile food and energy components. The results matched consensus forecasts from Reuters polls.
Over the last 12 months, CPI has risen 3.3 percent and only 2.6 percent on the core rate.
"We have an economy that is clicking right along but not so fast as to create excesses and stress in product markets," said Dederick, economic consultant at Northern Trust.
CPI continues to resist modest upward pressure from rising wages and energy prices, analysts noted.

Despite a 3.5 percent increase in average hourly earnings over the last 12 months and a low 5.4 percent unemployment rate that threatens to keep wages rising, analysts marvelled at the CPI's ability to absorb those pressures.
"Economists have been crying wolf about the fact that low unemployment creates higher inflation, but it hasn't," said Russell Sheldon, senior economist at Mellon Bank.
Yet as long as U.S. unemployment stays below 5.5 percent, Federal Reserve officials will remain wary of wage gains, Sheldon added.
The 5.5 percent level represents many economists' concept of the natural rate of unemployment, below which inflation will rise.

"We are right on the cusp and the Federal Reserve will be watching carefully. There is currently no impetus to move toward (monetary) restraint, but neither are things so good that they can consider easing policy," Sheldon said.

But the labor component of the economy should hold steady in months to come. Most analysts see inflation-adjusted gross domestic product rising by between 2.0 and 2.5 percent in 1997, which is generally considered the economy's maximum sustainable rate without accelerating inflation.
"I think its a continuation of fairly moderate inflation. Obviously there's a little more uneasiness about inflation given energy prices going up," said Larry Wipf, economist at Norwest Corp.
